\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four deficiencies in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across eight contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A power interpretation formalizes the onset as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$, generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$; sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).
    The MMCT exposes three pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from 20/24 significant at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.

    Predictive cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%) and fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation.

Other approaches track spectral divergence~\cite{sigma2026spectral}, topological features~\cite{kalinowski2026topology}, or center-edge sampling dynamics~\cite{dces2026counter}.
We differ from the closest predecessor, \citet{du2026geometric}, in four respects: (i)~we compare an entire family of canary metrics rather than a single pair; (ii)~we cross-validate across five independent statistical methods with inter-method sensitivity quantification; (iii)~we map detectability as a function of contamination regime; and (iv)~we treat method-selection sensitivity itself as a primary finding.

\paragraph{Early-warning signals and lead-lag methodology.}
The theoretical foundation for canary-based prediction originates in ecology: \citet{scheffer2009early} established that systems approaching tipping points exhibit generic early-warning signals, while \citet{boettiger2012limits} quantified detection limits in short time series---a constraint directly relevant to iterative training, where generation counts ($T{=}5$--$20$) are far smaller than typical ecological datasets.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four deficiencies in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across twelve contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A power interpretation formalizes the onset as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$, generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$; sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).
    The MMCT exposes three pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to 75\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from majority-significant at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    Predictive cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%) and fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation.
    A four-layer detection taxonomy provides regime-appropriate diagnostics from $\alpha{\geq}0.10$ to $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four deficiencies in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across twelve contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    \item \textbf{Signal-times-resolution theory} (\S\ref{sec:theory}).
    A power interpretation formalizes the onset as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$, generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$; sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).
    The MMCT exposes three pitfalls: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to 75\% ($\kappa{=}0.185$), first-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely while preserving all canary$\to$diversity leads (24/24$\to$24/24), and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from majority-significant at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$.
    PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse).

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    Predictive cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\% (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%) and fires one generation earlier than reactive cessation.
    A four-layer detection taxonomy provides regime-appropriate diagnostics from $\alpha{\geq}0.10$ to $\alpha{\geq}0.50$.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across twelve contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across six primary contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$ with multi-seed replication, plus six single-seed probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.60\}$) to resolve the onset boundary, yielding a 12-point $\alpha$ grid.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; remaining levels use a single seed (42).
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (Appendix).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
27	Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
28	Raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 is summarized in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary}.
29	
30	
31	\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
32	\label{sec:regime}
33	
34	Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
35	Despite this ubiquitous degradation, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
36	Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
37	This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
38	Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ (bootstrap 95\% CI: [0.43, 0.56]), steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (CI: [0.008, 0.060]), $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
39	The transition width is $6{\times}$ narrower than the estimation uncertainty in $\alpha_c$'s position, confirming a genuinely steep onset rather than an artifact of sparse sampling.
40	A model-free Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 21/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 1.65 \times 10^{-13}$).
41	At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
42	A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.
43	
44	First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
45	Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6 pairs per seed), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
46	All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
47	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 24 canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed $\times$ 4~seeds; mauve excluded) reach FDR significance in the forward direction with 0/24 reverse; directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
48	The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
49	Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable causal signal in the canary metrics.
50

53	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
54	\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed, mauve excluded).}
55	\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
56	\end{figure}
57	
58	
59	\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
60	\label{sec:dose_response}
61	
62	The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
63	The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
64	At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
65	The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across twelve contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across six primary contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$ with multi-seed replication, plus six single-seed probing points ($\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.60\}$) to resolve the onset boundary, yielding a 12-point $\alpha$ grid.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; remaining levels use a single seed (42).

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (Appendix).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
Raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 is summarized in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary}.


\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ (bootstrap 95\% CI: [0.43, 0.56]), steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$ (CI: [0.008, 0.060]), $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
The transition width is $6{\times}$ narrower than the estimation uncertainty in $\alpha_c$'s position, confirming a genuinely steep onset rather than an artifact of sparse sampling.
A model-free Fisher exact test corroborates the categorical jump: 0/64 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha \leq 0.45$ versus 21/32 at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ ($p = 1.65 \times 10^{-13}$).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6 pairs per seed), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 24 canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed $\times$ 4~seeds; mauve excluded) reach FDR significance in the forward direction with 0/24 reverse; directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).
Below $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$, diversity collapse proceeds without any detectable causal signal in the canary metrics.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{Metric trajectories at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds). Token entropy drops at generation~1; distinct-1 declines from generations~2--3, with a consistent one-generation canary lead across all four seeds (shaded: inter-seed range). This pattern corresponds to 24/24 forward and 0/24 reverse FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs (6 per seed, mauve excluded).}
\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Dose-Response and the $S \times R$ Framework}
\label{sec:dose_response}

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, 0/8 both seeds; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, direction-checked forward significance rates span 0\% to 75\%: naive and differenced cross-correlation fall to 0/8 after lag-direction filtering (all significant correlations peak at negative lags), while PermG achieves 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}). Inter-method agreement is $\kappa{=}0.185$ (near chance).
PermG is the only method that combines zero null-control FPR with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}); its nonparametric null distribution, built-in directionality, and hyperparameter-free design explain this advantage.
The $S \times R$ framework generates three testable predictions for $T{=}20$ via $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ should left-shift, (ii)~the transition should smooth, and (iii)~different methods should exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values.
These predictions are under empirical verification.

\caption{PermG forward detection rate across 12 contamination levels (Pythia-410M, fp32, direction-checked). Four regimes: blind ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8), onset ($\alpha{=}0.50$, 6/8), synchronous dip ($\alpha{=}0.60$, 0--3/8), and detection ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8).}
\label{fig:regime_map}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering

\label{tab:method_comparison}

\end{tabular}
\end{table}


\subsection{Cross-Architecture Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

We evaluate the detection phase transition across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B parameters, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} reports PermG forward detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}$6/8 in 13 of 15 conditions (87\%).
Two exceptions emerge: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 on WikiText (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs reach significance while entropy$\to$downstream pairs fail entirely (0/4; details in Appendix).

The onset boundary $\alpha_c \approx 0.50$ at $T{=}10$ is architecture-independent: every family that achieves detection does so at or above this threshold, and none achieves reliable detection below it.

Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection observed: Pythia-1B reaches PermG fwd 8/8 (both seeds), and Pythia-1.4B reaches 8/8 on C4 versus 2/8 on WikiText at the same scale.
At Pythia-6.9B (bf16), detection recovers to 7/8 on WikiText.
Dataset characteristics modulate detection power independently of model capacity.
Directional asymmetry shows preliminary domain variation: in one C4 seed-condition pair ($\alpha{=}0.50$, s42), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, but this is seed-dependent (s43: 1/8) and we note it as a preliminary observation requiring further investigation (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\subsection{Detection Phase Transition}
\label{sec:regime}

Diversity collapse occurs at every contamination level: distinct-1 declines by $14.1\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (fine-tuning drift) and by $40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (3-seed mean).
Despite this ubiquitous degradation, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent.
Permutation Granger (PermG) tests find 0/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jump to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent).
This transition is striking because cumulative synthetic fraction barely changes across the boundary: $C = 1{-}(1{-}\alpha)^{10}$ yields $99.75\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ versus $99.90\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a difference of 0.15 percentage points, yet detection jumps from null to reliable.
Sigmoid regression across the 12-point $\alpha$ grid quantifies this steep onset: $\alpha_c = 0.476$ at $T{=}10$, steepness $k \geq 200$, transition width $\Delta\alpha \approx 0.02$, $R^2 = 0.969$ (versus power-law $R^2 = 0.808$, $\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = 18.2$; Figure~\ref{fig:phase_transition}).
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, PermG $p$-values reveal sub-threshold signal ($p_{\mathrm{fdr}} = 0.059$ for seed~43, $0.091$ for seed~42), consistent with the power-threshold interpretation of $\alpha_c$ at $T{=}10$ (\S\ref{sec:theory}): the onset reflects PermG's power curve crossing the detection floor, not the emergence of a new physical signal.
A specification curve analysis spanning 1{,}160 analytical specifications confirms that the detection phase transition is specification-invariant.

First-differencing scopes the canary claim precisely.
Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing ($24/24 \to 24/24$ across 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), while canary$\to$perplexity collapses entirely ($F \approx 0$, $p = 0.99$): the apparent perplexity association is a shared-trend artifact.
All canary claims are therefore scoped to diversity metrics only.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, 24/24 forward-direction pairs reach FDR significance with 0/24 reverse (4~seeds); directional asymmetry is robust across all WikiText conditions.
The canary mechanism also exhibits a blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, distinct-1 has already dropped by $39.6\%$, yet token entropy is indistinguishable from the null ($-5.3\%$ versus $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$).

The PermG dose-response profile (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}) reveals four detection regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$, 0/8 FDR-significant pairs), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$, 6/8), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$, s42: 3/8, s43: 0/8; dual-seed confirmed), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$, 5--6/8 per seed across 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$, 6/8 across 4~seeds).
The non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ is consistent with the $S \times R$ framework (\S\ref{sec:theory}): signal strength $S(\alpha)$ rises monotonically with contamination, but temporal resolution $R(\alpha)$ drops when relaxation time approaches the observation interval.
At $\alpha \approx 0.60$, this compression drives the canary-to-downstream lag toward zero, and the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind zone, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.

Method choice is itself a major source of analytic variability.
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, forward-direction significance rates range from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (PermG), with inter-method $\kappa = 0.185$ (near chance) and a spurious rate of at least 62.5\%.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
\label{sec:pitfalls}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs, direction-checked) yield forward significance rates spanning 0\% to 75\%, with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and naive cross-correlation reaching 75\% null-control FPR.
\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.

\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
\label{sec:mmct}
We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method.
It compares five lead-lag detection methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
Each method $m_k$ receives weight $w_k = 1/\max(\hat{\text{FPR}}_k, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon{=}0.01$; the weighted score $W(X \to Y) = \sum_k w_k d_k / \sum_k w_k$ yields formal $p$-values from the empirical null distribution (Appendix).
MMCT identifies permutation Granger (PermG) as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across contamination levels, and we recommend it as the primary detection method based on this systematic comparison.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history; Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We apply 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics).
Three properties distinguish PermG: a nonparametric null distribution robust to the short non-stationary series typical of iterative training~\cite{boettiger2012limits}, built-in directionality (forward and reverse tested separately), and a hyperparameter-free test statistic.
The remaining four methods each exhibit a specific limitation: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR; differenced cross-correlation detects bidirectionally without directional separation; threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (0/8 significant in 8 of 12 cross-architecture conditions); Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical} achieves moderate supplementary detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power from degree-of-freedom costs of lag augmentation.
Per-method dose-response profiles, Shapley value analysis, and the full MMCT algorithm appear in the Appendix.

\subsection{Signal-Times-Resolution Framework}
\label{sec:theory}

We apply standard statistical power scaling to PermG under the Signal$\times$Resolution (S$\times$R) framework.
Detectability of canary$\to$downstream temporal precedence depends on two competing factors:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Detectability}(\alpha) \;\propto\; S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha),
    \label{eq:detectability}
\end{equation}
where $S(\alpha)$ is signal strength (magnitude of distributional shift, monotonically increasing with $\alpha$) and $R(\alpha)$ is temporal resolution (the generational gap between canary and downstream responses).
$R(\alpha)$ is non-monotonic: at low $\alpha$, entropy and diversity respond in different generations ($R$ large); at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$, relaxation time matching compresses both responses into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at high $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the diversity cascade, restoring the generational offset.
The product $S \times R$ predicts four regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; $S$ below detection floor), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$; $S$ crosses threshold while $R$ remains high), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$; $R \to 0$ suppresses detection despite rising $S$), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$; $S$ dominates).
Full empirical confirmation appears in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.

Under a permutation test framework, detection power scales as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T} / \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF and the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling follows standard power analysis.
The detection phase transition at $\alpha_c$ (at $T{=}10$) is consistent with a power threshold: when $S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}$ first exceeds the detection floor, power undergoes a steep onset from near-zero to near-one.
This generates three predictions for $T{=}20$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ left-shifts as increased $T$ raises power at all $\alpha$; (ii)~the transition smooths as $\sqrt{T}$ broadens the power curve; (iii)~different methods exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values due to method-specific power curves.
The key falsifiable test is the sub-threshold prediction: the framework predicts 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (at $T{=}10$), confirmed empirically (\S\ref{sec:regime}), with sub-threshold FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$ consistent with proximity to the power boundary.
Detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (predicted ${\geq}5/8$, CI${=}[5,8]$) serves as supplementary consistency evidence rather than a strong test, as these predictions are near-unfalsifiable given signal strength.

\paragraph{Calibration.}
We validate error rates with built-in experimental controls.
False positive rate: at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control, no synthetic contamination), PermG and MMCT weighted consensus both yield 0\% FPR across 3 seeds (0/24 pairs at consensus $K{\geq}3$).
False negative rate: at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all 6 effect-size reference pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 3 diversity metrics, selected by criteria independent of the detection methods) are recovered at 0\% FNR across 4 seeds.
PermG matches consensus performance at all tested contamination levels, with cross-architecture validation confirming PermG forward significance ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
Full calibration details, practical guidance tiers, and method-level breakdown appear in the Appendix.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
\label{sec:pitfalls}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yield significance rates from 100\% (naive cross-correlation) to 37.5\% (permutation Granger), with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and a spurious-signal rate ${\geq}62.5\%$.
\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.

\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
\label{sec:mmct}
We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method.
It compares five lead-lag detection methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
Each method $m_k$ receives weight $w_k = 1/\max(\hat{\text{FPR}}_k, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon{=}0.01$; the weighted score $W(X \to Y) = \sum_k w_k d_k / \sum_k w_k$ yields formal $p$-values from the empirical null distribution (Algorithm~\ref{alg:mmct}; Appendix).
MMCT identifies permutation Granger (PermG) as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across contamination levels, and we recommend it as the primary detection method based on this systematic comparison.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history; Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We apply 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics).
Three properties distinguish PermG: a nonparametric null distribution robust to the short non-stationary series typical of iterative training~\cite{boettiger2012limits}, built-in directionality (forward and reverse tested separately), and a hyperparameter-free test statistic.
The remaining four methods each exhibit a specific limitation: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR; differenced cross-correlation detects bidirectionally without directional separation; threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (0/8 significant in 8 of 12 cross-architecture conditions); Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical} achieves moderate supplementary detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power from degree-of-freedom costs of lag augmentation.
Per-method dose-response profiles, Shapley value analysis, and the full MMCT algorithm appear in the Appendix.

\subsection{Signal-Times-Resolution Framework}
\label{sec:theory}

We apply standard statistical power scaling to PermG under the Signal$\times$Resolution (S$\times$R) framework.
Detectability of canary$\to$downstream temporal precedence depends on two competing factors:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Detectability}(\alpha) \;\propto\; S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha),
    \label{eq:detectability}
\end{equation}
where $S(\alpha)$ is signal strength (magnitude of distributional shift, monotonically increasing with $\alpha$) and $R(\alpha)$ is temporal resolution (the generational gap between canary and downstream responses).
$R(\alpha)$ is non-monotonic: at low $\alpha$, entropy and diversity respond in different generations ($R$ large); at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$, relaxation time matching compresses both responses into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at high $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the diversity cascade, restoring the generational offset.
The product $S \times R$ predicts four regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; $S$ below detection floor), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$; $S$ crosses threshold while $R$ remains high), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$; $R \to 0$ suppresses detection despite rising $S$), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$; $S$ dominates).
Full empirical confirmation appears in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.

Under a permutation test framework, detection power scales as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T} / \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF and the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling follows standard power analysis.
The detection phase transition at $\alpha_c$ (at $T{=}10$) is consistent with a power threshold: when $S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}$ first exceeds the detection floor, power undergoes a steep onset from near-zero to near-one.
This generates three predictions for $T{=}20$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ left-shifts as increased $T$ raises power at all $\alpha$; (ii)~the transition smooths as $\sqrt{T}$ broadens the power curve; (iii)~different methods exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values due to method-specific power curves.
The key falsifiable test is the sub-threshold prediction: the framework predicts 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.45$ (at $T{=}10$), confirmed empirically (\S\ref{sec:regime}), with sub-threshold FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$ consistent with proximity to the power boundary.
Detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (predicted ${\geq}5/8$, CI${=}[5,8]$) serves as supplementary consistency evidence rather than a strong test, as these predictions are near-unfalsifiable given signal strength.

\paragraph{Calibration.}
We validate error rates with built-in experimental controls.
False positive rate: at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control, no synthetic contamination), PermG and MMCT weighted consensus both yield 0\% FPR across 3 seeds (0/24 pairs at consensus $K{\geq}3$).

PermG matches consensus performance at all tested contamination levels, with cross-architecture validation confirming PermG forward significance ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
Full calibration details, practical guidance tiers, and method-level breakdown appear in the Appendix.
